The US has declared a blockade of Iranian ports and fired on a Panama-flagged ship that violated it; Trump claims 'total control' over the Strait of Hormuz. Hormuz traffic has fallen to a new low. The conflict has spread to the Red Sea, where a Houthi attack killed 6 people — the first Red Sea fatalities in over a year — including 3 Pakistani nationals; the US has struck a containership in the area. Iran continues to condition reopening the Strait on unmet demands. Qatar says Oman-Iran negotiations over shipping are making major progress. Pakistan's defense minister had earlier said the US and Iran were close to some arrangement, while Pakistan's foreign minister condemned the Houthi attacks. Trump reportedly hid in a catering truck to evade an assassination threat after the NATO summit. Oil had surged ~3% above $83/barrel, with further rises on Red Sea supply concerns.

Separately, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt has announced she will step down at the end of the month to focus on her family, including a newborn second child. Trump confirmed the departure and said she will continue as an outside adviser.

Separately, a major Ebola crisis is unfolding in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The WHO warns the outbreak — caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there are no approved vaccines or treatments — is on track to become the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history. The UN Secretary-General says cases are doubling every 20 days, threatening to eclipse the 2014-2016 West African epidemic. WHO has revealed the outbreak spread undetected for months, suggesting its true scale is far larger than official counts. Over 2,000 people have been killed.

Peggy Flanagan won the Democratic Senate primary by 20 points over moderate Rep. Angie Craig, in a race defined by anti-ICE anger following the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. Flanagan, backed by Bernie Sanders and Ilhan Omar, could become the first Native woman in the Senate. Her win is the latest in a series of progressive victories over moderates in the Midwest — including Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan U.S. Senate primary win the prior week — and marks a second straight primary setback for Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer. Flanagan faces baggage from a Minnesota fraud scandal that occurred during her tenure as Lt. Gov. Former TV sports reporter Michele Tafoya won the Republican Senate primary in Minnesota and will face Flanagan in November. Minnesota is the first state to set all-female matchups in both its biggest races: Flanagan vs. Tafoya for Senate, and Klobuchar vs. Demuth for governor. Ilhan Omar has been projected to win the Democratic primary in Minnesota's 5th Congressional District. Sen. Amy Klobuchar has been projected to win the Minnesota DFL gubernatorial primary and will face Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth in November; Demuth defeated Trump-backed MyPillow founder Mike Lindell, who received roughly 31% of the vote. Post-loss, Lindell questioned the vote numbers. In Minnesota's 1st Congressional District, GOP incumbent Brad Finstad survived a primary against challengers Gregory Goetzman and Oliver Morlan. In Connecticut, former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin has been projected to defeat veteran Democratic incumbent Rep. John Larson in the House primary. Larson's loss makes him the 10th House incumbent to lose a primary this cycle, an unusually high figure driven by Democrats pushing leaders to pass the torch to a younger, more progressive generation and Republicans reckoning with Trump's influence. In Wisconsin, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley defeated democratic socialist Francesca Hong in a stunningly narrow Democratic gubernatorial primary — winning by less than a percentage point — after re-entering the race and securing an endorsement from outgoing Gov. Tony Evers, who called Crowley 'the future of the party.' Crowley, who could become the state's first Black governor, will face Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in November. Following her loss, Hong endorsed Crowley. Sabato's Crystal Ball subsequently shifted the Wisconsin governor's race toward Democrats. In South Carolina's special GOP Senate primary, Darline Graham (32.6%) and Rep. Ralph Norman (24%) have advanced to an Aug. 25 runoff, with Rep. Russell Fry finishing third at 20.3%. Trump-backed Graham denied being a 'nepo senator.' Trump's endorsements have broadly flopped in major statewide governor races: in addition to Lindell, Trump-backed Andy Ogles (TN) and Amir Hassan (MI) also lost their primaries; Hassan lost to Thomas Smith. An analysis by G. Elliott Morris found that primary election polls miss by an average of 13 points, and prediction markets were also shown to have failed on the Hong result in Wisconsin.
